newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar shaken by report in weak market.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar shaken by report in weak market.

text.p: The typically staid Singapore dollar was briefly jolted on Friday, as market players reacted to a local newspaper headline amid growing talk of an economic slowdown in the city-state.

Dealers said the U.S. dollar was pushed up above resistance at S$1.4150 in early trade in response to a Business Times report quoting Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong on the gradual internationalisation of the Singapore dollar.
Goh was quoted as saying this would help local companies to do business outside Singapore in an article headlined, "Gradual Sing $ easing will help local companies: PM."
"When people looked at the headline, they thought (it meant) the Sing dollar should weaken," said a Japanese bank dealer, adding that this had spurred a round of ringgit/Sing buying.

Noting that the text of the article suggested an easing of controls on the currency, the dealer said, "the buying was basically interbank players speculating...taking a short punt after seeing the headline."

"It was a knee-jerk reaction to the headline," said Andy Tan, economist and general manager at MMS International, adding, however, that buying interest in the Singapore dollar had limited its weakness to 1.4155. It was quoted at 1.4146/51 against the U.S. dollar at 0825 GMT.
"When a currency's internationalised, it implies there would be more demand for it," Tan said.
He said Goh's comment pointed to a possible gradual strengthening of the Singapore dollar. "If you have a weak currency, there's less incentive for local firms to move offshore," he added.

Dealers said the Singapore dollar was also weighed down by a bullish U.S. dollar and expectations of slowing economic growth on the back of recent declines in industrial production and non-oil export growth.
Tan said the Singapore dollar was likely to recover to 1.4130/40 to the U.S. dollar unless September's export data, due early next week, were unexpectedly weak.
"If there's a double-digit decline in non-oil exports, then the Sing dollar could weaken to 1.42," he said. "But if it's just a 3-4 percent decline, I don't think there'll be much impact."
A Reuters poll of 12 financial institutions produced an average forecast of a 3.4 percent year-on-year decline in non-oil exports for September in nominal terms.
This compares with a fall of 6.3 percent in August and a rise of 6.3 percent in July.
